# Ask Conversation Scope

## How To Build

A AskConversationScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A AskConversationScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

The questions asked from the Ask tab, read as a chat: every question and its answer, one after another, in a pane of its own beside the tasks, with each new conversation clearly marked where it begins.

### Shape

#### Description

While the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope)'s Ask tab is selected, the [BodyScope](../../application/Body.md#body-scope) splits in two, side by side, above the chat input: the body's tab bar and the selected tab's contents on the left, and this pane on the right. It goes when another tab is selected, the left side taking the body's full width again, and comes back as it was, scrolled where it was, when Ask is selected again. Nothing slides as it comes and goes.
It is drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope)'s roles, on the same base surface as the selected tab's contents beside it, with the theme's line between the two halves. Along its top runs a header as tall as the body's tab bar, 32 pixels, on the tab bar's background with the theme's line beneath it, reading "Questions" at its left, with 12 pixels of padding, and at its right how many questions it holds, muted.

#### Split

The pane starts at half the width of the space it shares with the left side. The line between them is a resize edge: hovering it shows the resize cursor for left and right and a thin line in the theme's accent, and dragging it moves it, following the pointer exactly, from 25% to 75% of that space, both sides laid out anew at each width. The width it is dragged to is kept for as long as the application runs, for every project, and none of it is saved.

#### Conversation

The pane lists every question of the project, those saved with it and those asked since, running or finished, oldest at the top and the newest at the bottom, the way a chat reads. Each is a message and its reply. The question is shown as it was typed, not as it was compiled, in a box on the theme's raised surface, faintly tinted Ask's colour, as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours it, with corners rounded 6 pixels, set against the pane's right edge and at most 80% of its width, wrapping within that, with anything it was sent with, attached text and images, listed beneath its text as the chat input lists them. Beneath the box, at its right, sits a small muted line with the time it was asked and, once it is finished, a Resend button, which asks the question again as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says, the new question coming in at the bottom.
Its answer follows beneath it, as a chat reply rather than a task: against the pane's left edge, across the pane's full width, with no box. The answer is read as prose, not as a list of what the harness did.

#### Answers

An answer is not drawn as a [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope): it has no columns, no Type badges or Status labels, and no lines between rows. What is shown is the answer's reply text, the reply rows after the harness's last tool call, as the table's collapsed steps count them, rendered as markdown in the body's text colour, one paragraph after another, as a message in a chat is. Code blocks, lists, tables, and links in it are rendered as markdown renders them anywhere. An answer with no tool calls is all reply text; a finished answer with nothing to show reads "No answer.", muted.
Everything the harness did before the answer, its tool calls and any reply text between them, is gathered into one line above the answer, small and muted, beside a right chevron, summing it up, as "Read 3 files, searched twice, ran 1 command" or "Worked through 6 steps" where it can't be summed up by kind. Clicking it expands the steps in place, beneath it and above the answer, as compact muted lines, one per step: a tool call as its tool's name, muted, then its most telling argument, shortened as the [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope)'s tool calls are, and reply text between them as muted markdown; clicking it again collapses them. It starts collapsed, and stays as it was left for as long as the application runs. An answer whose harness did nothing before replying has no such line.
While the harness works on a question, a status line takes that line's place: a spinner and the latest thing the harness did, muted, with a Stop button at its right that stops just that question, leaving the others running. Reply text streams in beneath it as prose as the harness writes it; text it goes on to follow with a tool call joins the steps once the call comes, so only the answer is left as prose. Once the question finishes, the status line becomes the summary line.
A question that failed ends its answer with the error, in the theme's error colour, beneath whatever reply came before it. One that was stopped ends with "Stopped", muted. Neither is shown as a status in a table.
Questions are 16 pixels apart, and a question's answer 8 pixels beneath it.
Questions asked while another is still running come in at the bottom in the order they were asked, each answered in its own place as its harness goes, so answers can be filling in at once.

#### New Conversation

Where a new conversation begins, it is clearly marked: above the first question of each conversation, the first question in the pane included, runs a divider across the pane's full width, a line in Ask's colour at either side of a label reading "New conversation", then, muted, the date and time its first question was asked. A question starts a new conversation as its saved record says, in its hidden anchor's newConversation, as the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) says; a question saved before that was recorded carries on the one above it, unless it is the first. A question asked while another was running carries on a copy of that conversation, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, and is not marked.
Pressing New conversation for questions puts the divider in at the bottom of the pane straight away, beneath the last question, reading "New conversation" with no time, so it is plain that the next question starts with no context; the time is filled in once that question is asked. Pressed again with nothing asked since, it adds no second divider.

#### Scrolling

The pane scrolls, with a [ScrollbarScope](../../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar-scope), and opens scrolled to the bottom, on the newest question, the first time it is shown. While it is at the bottom it stays locked there, following each question asked and each answer as it grows; scrolling up unlocks it, and scrolling back to the bottom locks it again. Asking a question always scrolls it to the bottom and locks it. However many questions it holds, and however long their answers, it lays out only what is in view: each question, divider, summary line, and block of an answer's markdown is drawn as it scrolls into view, so a long conversation costs no more to show, scroll, or resize than a short one.

#### Empty

With no question asked yet, the pane reads "No questions yet. Ask one below.", muted, centred in it.

#### Selecting Text

The text of any question, answer, or expanded step in the pane can be selected by dragging across it, as any text can. A drag that selects text ending within the pane shows a [SelectionPopoverScope](../../../ui/components/selection-popover/index.md#selection-popover-scope) with two buttons, "Copy", with a copy icon, and "Attach to prompt", with a paperclip icon. Copy puts the selected text on the clipboard; Attach to prompt adds it to the prompt as an attachment. Either one clears the selection, and the popover closes when the pane goes.

#### Elsewhere

While another tab is selected, the questions still running stay in view as small rows stacked directly above the chat input's tabs, the newest nearest them, each showing its first line and the latest thing the harness did, in a column that pushes what is above it up rather than covering it, up to 240 pixels tall and scrolling beyond that. A question leaves the stack once it finishes. Clicking one selects the Ask tab, the pane scrolled to that question. There is no stack while Ask is selected: its questions are in the pane.

#### Projects

The pane shows the questions of the project on screen, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope) says, and each project keeps how far its pane was scrolled and whether it was locked to the bottom while the application runs; questions of other projects carry on running in the background.

# Prompt Modes Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

The modes a prompt is sent in, each for a different kind of work on the code and the spec.

### Shape

#### Description

There are five modes, and wherever they are listed, they are in this order.

#### Modes

- Code: changes the code, leaving the spec as it is; a subtle red
- Chain: changes the code and the spec together; purple
- Spec: changes the spec, leaving the code as it is; a subtle blue
- Ask: asks a question about the code and the spec, changing neither; a subtle green
- Freeform: passes the prompt to the agent just as it is written; grey, the theme's tertiary text colour

#### Colours

Whatever shows a mode, or something sent in it, takes the mode's colour, a tint of the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope)'s hue of that name, readable in both light and dark mode. Chain is Code and Spec together, so wherever it shows Code and Spec as well, both are purple: the colour midway between Code's and Spec's. A colour chosen for Code, Chain, Spec, or Ask in the theme edit

#### Tasks

A prompt sent in Code, Chain, Spec, or Freeform is a task, sent as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. Tasks carry on one conversation, and run in two lanes, as it says: Code tasks in the code lane and Spec tasks in the spec lane, each queueing only behind tasks of its own lane, so a Spec task runs beside a Code task rather than waiting for it. A Chain task's s

#### Questions

A prompt sent in Ask is a question. It runs straight away, alongside any task and any other question, and never queues, builds the spec, or adds a commit note. concept ModeSystemPromptsConcept:
    pitch:

        work a prompt is, and which each project can make its own.

    shape: {ModeSystemPromptsShape}

shape ModeSystemPromptsShape:
    description:
        What a prompt tells the harness besides itself comes in two parts. The
        system template is the conversation's system prompt: the same for
        every prompt of a conversation, whatever its mode, so the harness's
        prompt cache holds when the mode changes. Each lane's tasks, and the
        questions, carry on a conversation of their own, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, and each fills the system template in
        for what its runs can see, so it stays the same within each. Each of the
        @{PromptModesScope} but Freeform has instructions of its own, which
        change from one prompt to the next, and so go in the prompt's own
        message, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head. A
        prompt's hidden anchor has a systemPrompt property, alongside its
        userPrompt, holding its mode's instructions.

    templates:
        The system template, each mode's instructions, and the injected
        prompts are Piton prose, like the prompt they are sent with, so they
        can reference the spec, with these placeholders, each written after a
        dollar sign and inside braces like a Piton interpolation:

        - CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION, the code location and the spec location, as the @{ProjectLocationsScope} says
        - HARNESS_DIRECTORY, the directory of the harness in use
        - SPEC_READING, the spec-reading prompt, injected where it is written
        - PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, the path of the fluency file, from the project directory, as the pitonFluency below says
        - UNDERSTANDING_FILE, the path of the task's understanding file

        SPEC_READING is filled in first, so the placeholders it holds are
        filled in too; then the others, before the prompt is compiled, but
        UNDERSTANDING_FILE, which is filled in as the prompt is sent, once the
        task's history record is named, so a prompt sent from the queue is
        given its own. A question from the Ask tab has no understanding file,
        and UNDERSTANDING_FILE is filled in with nothing. Each can be moved or
        removed, like any other text of a template.

        is sent it finds that file, whether it runs on the host or in a
        container, as the @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says. So each is
        written relative to the project directory, the directory every run
        works in, the project directory itself on the host and `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`
        in a container: CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION as `./` and the
        location's path, as `./spec`, HARNESS_DIRECTORY as the harness's
        directory, as `.claude`, and PITON_FLUENCY_FILE and
        UNDERSTANDING_FILE as their paths, as
        `.suspense/fluency.md`. None is ever filled in with an absolute path:
        not the project's path on the host, which a run in a container can't
        reach, and not `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`, which a run on the host has no such
        directory for.

        A run fills CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION in only with what it can
        see, as the @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says. A run of the spec
        lane, a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step, can't see the code
        location, and fills CODE_LOCATION in with nothing, its instructions and
        system template alike. A question can see the code location and the
        spec location, both read only, and fills both in. A run of the code
        lane, a Code task, a Chain prompt's code step, or a Freeform task,
        runs on the host and fills both in, as ever.

        A paragraph that held nothing but a placeholder filled in with
        nothing goes with it. A paragraph holding CODE_LOCATION or
        SPEC_LOCATION filled in with nothing goes too, whatever else it says,
        so no prompt names, or tells the harness to keep off, a location its
        run can't see. A paragraph holding PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, filled
        in with nothing, goes too, whatever else it says, so a sentence
        pointing at a fluency file there is none of is never sent. A template
        left with nothing but blank space once filled in gives nothing at
        all.

        HARNESS_DIRECTORY is the directory the harness that runs the prompt,
        as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, reads its agentic Markdown and
        reference files from, written without a leading ./: .claude for
        Claude Code, .opencode for OpenCode, and .codex for Codex, the
        directories the @{NewProjectScope} names for them.

    readingTheSpec:
        In every mode, the harness learns what the spec says from its
        compiled reference, the Markdown the spec build writes under
        HARNESS_DIRECTORY's reference folder, where inheritance, expressions,
        and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what
        `piton slice` prints for it with the adapter of the harness in use.
        It never reads the Piton source under the spec location to learn what
        the spec says. To a run that can see the spec location, the system
        template and the spec-reading prompt say so, and name the spec
        location only as where edits to the spec go. A question sees the spec
        location too, read only, so it can run `piton slice` there, and is
        told the same: that the spec is read from the compiled reference or
        from what `piton slice` prints, never from the Piton source. A
        question makes no edits, so the Ask instructions name the spec
        location for what it is, the spec's Piton source, that `piton slice`
        reads, which a question never changes, and nothing told to a question

        spec location is told only that the spec is read from the compiled
        reference, with nothing about the spec source.

        work on the Piton source. Their instructions say to open a .pi file
        only to change it, since a harness may need a file read before it can
        edit it, and, once the edits are made, to run `piton build` and check
        the result in the refreshed reference rather than by reading the
        source again.

        the project directory, is how Piton is written. It is never part of
        the system prompt: only work that writes Piton is pointed at it.

        project's data, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, each time the
        application runs a spec build in the project, as the @{SpecBuildScope}

        ever been written has it written before the prompt is compiled. What
        it prints is written as text, never read as Piton, but for the
        project directory's absolute path on the host wherever it appears in
        it, which is written as `.` instead, a path within it as relative to
        it, as `./spec`, so the file holds no path a run in a container
        can't reach.

        and the Chain instructions, for a Chain prompt's first step, say, on a
        paragraph of their own, to read that file once in the conversation
        before creating or editing any .pi file. A Code task sent to Spec
        is pointed at it through the Spec instructions, as any Spec prompt is.
        The Code and Ask instructions, and the spec-to-code prompt given to a
        Chain prompt's code step, never mention it.

        is written, and PITON_FLUENCY_FILE is filled in with nothing, so the
        paragraph pointing at it is left out.

        The spec-reading prompt explains how to read the spec before executing
        anything, as the readingTheSpec above says: from the compiled
        reference, reference links in the prompt being the spec for what they
        name, each read before anything it covers is changed. It is injected
        into the system template wherever SPEC_READING is written, and may
        itself use every placeholder but SPEC_READING, which in it is left as
        written. One left with nothing but blank space leaves SPEC_READING
        filled in with nothing. Like the templates, each project has its own,
        saved with its data, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, in
        spec-reading.md beside them, and edited in the
        @{SettingsWindowScope}; with no file yet the project uses its default.

    codeToSpec:
        The code-to-spec prompt is given to a Code task sent to Spec, as the
        @{PromptSendingScope} says, after the Spec instructions. It may use
        every placeholder the instructions may, filled in the same way, and
        two of its own: CODE_PROMPT, filled in with the code task's prompt as
        it was typed, and CODE_RESULT, with the code task's final output, or
        with a line saying the code task left none. What fills them in is
        taken as text, never read as Piton. Like the spec-reading prompt, each
        project has its own, saved with its data in code-to-spec.md beside the
        templates, and edited in the @{SettingsWindowScope}; with no file yet
        the project uses its default.

        The spec-to-code prompt is given in the same way to the code step a
        Chain prompt hands on to, after the Code instructions, with
        SPEC_PROMPT and SPEC_RESULT, the Chain prompt as it was typed and its
        spec step's final output, saved in spec-to-code.md.

    saving:
        Each project has its own system template, instructions, and injected
        prompts, saved with its data, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, a
        Markdown file each, system.md for the system template, code.md,
        combined.md for Chain, spec.md, and ask.md for the modes, and edited
        in the @{SettingsWindowScope}. One with no file yet gives its default.

    understandingFile:
        Each Code, Chain, or Spec task has an understanding file: the short
        list of constraints the harness has taken from the spec for it, which
        the @{RightSidebarScope} shows as it changes. It is saved
        beside the task's history record, with the same name and the
        extension `.understanding.md`, written by the harness itself. Nothing
        else writes it, and nothing is there until the harness writes it. Each
        constraint links to the compiled reference file it comes from, never
        to the spec's source.

    defaults:
        The defaults are the prompts saved in this application's own
        repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, named as a
        project's are. They are the source of truth for the defaults, and are
        baked into the application when it is built, so a build always ships
        with whatever those files say, and changing them changes the defaults
        the next build has. A build can't be made without them.

        The system template's default says what the project is, where its
        code is and where its spec is, each on a paragraph of its own, so the
        one a run can't see goes, that each prompt starts with a
        <task-instructions> block saying what that prompt is for and what it
        may change, and then SPEC_READING on a paragraph of its own. It holds
        no fluency.

        The spec-reading prompt's default says:

        \\
        Read the spec from its compiled reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter.

        Never read the .pi source under ${SPEC_LOCATION} to learn what the spec says; that is only where edits to the spec go.

        Before executing anything, read the spec it touches. Links to ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/... in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one you need before changing anything it covers. Don't re-read something you've already read.
        \\

        The Spec and Chain defaults have, after what the mode is for, on a
        paragraph of its own:

        \\
        Before creating or editing any .pi file, read ${PITON_FLUENCY_FILE} once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.
        \\

        and then, on another:

        \\
        Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, not by reading the source again.
        \\

        The Code, Chain, and Spec defaults then end with, on a paragraph of
        its own:

        \\
        Before changing anything, write the constraints this task must meet to ${UNDERSTANDING_FILE}, and keep it current as you read more of the spec. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.
        \\

        The Ask default says what a question is for, and that it changes
        nothing, and, on a paragraph of its own, that SPEC_LOCATION is the
        spec's Piton source, there for `piton slice`, which the question reads
        the spec through, read only and never edited, and never read directly
        to learn what the spec says. Since a question can see the spec
        location, that paragraph is always sent with it. The Spec and Chain
        defaults never name the code location, and the Code default names the
        spec location only on a paragraph of its own, which goes where the run
        can't see it.

        The defaults are only where a project starts, and what resetting a
        prompt puts back. A project whose prompts were saved before a default
        changed keeps them as they are.

        and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what
        `piton slice` prints for it with the adapter of the harness in use.
        It never reads the Piton source under the spec location to learn what
        the spec says. To a run that can see the spec location, the system
        template and the spec-reading prompt say so, and name the spec
        location only as where edits to the spec go. A question sees the spec
        location too, read only, so it can run `piton slice` there, and is
        told the same: that the spec is read from the compiled reference or
        from what `piton slice` prints, never from the Piton source. A
        question makes no edits, so the Ask instructions name the spec
        location for what it is, the spec's Piton source, that `piton slice`
        reads, which a question never changes, and nothing told to a question
        says or suggests that it may edit the spec. A run that can't see the
        spec location is told only that the spec is read from the compiled
        reference, with nothing about the spec source.

    writingTheSpec:
        Only Spec, and a Chain prompt's first step, which writes the spec,
        work on the Piton source. Their instructions say to open a .pi file
        only to change it, since a harness may need a file read before it can
        edit it, and, once the edits are made, to run `piton build` and check
        the result in the refreshed reference rather than by reading the
        source again.

    pitonFluency:
        The Piton fluency, what `piton agent --print-fluency` prints, run in
        the project directory, is how Piton is written. It is never part of
        the system prompt: only work that writes Piton is pointed at it.

        It is written to the fluency file, `.suspense/fluency.md` in the
        project's data, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, each time the
        application runs a spec build in the project, as the @{SpecBuildScope}
        says, so it keeps in step with the project's piton and its
        FLUENCY_PROMPT.md. A Spec or Chain prompt sent before the file has
        ever been written has it written before the prompt is compiled. What
        it prints is written as text, never read as Piton, but for the
        project directory's absolute path on the host wherever it appears in
        it, which is written as `.` instead, a path within it as relative to
        it, as `./spec`, so the file holds no path a run in a container
        can't reach.

        PITON_FLUENCY_FILE stands for the file's path. The Spec instructions
        and the Chain instructions, for a Chain prompt's first step, say, on a
        paragraph of their own, to read that file once in the conversation
        before creating or editing any .pi file. A Code task sent to Spec
        is pointed at it through the Spec instructions, as any Spec prompt is.
        The Code and Ask instructions, and the spec-to-code prompt given to a
        Chain prompt's code step, never mention it.

        Where `piton` isn't installed, or printing the fluency fails, no file
        is written, and PITON_FLUENCY_FILE is filled in with nothing, so the
        paragraph pointing at it is left out.

    specReading:
        The spec-reading prompt explains how to read the spec before executing
        anything, as the readingTheSpec above says: from the compiled
        reference, reference links in the prompt being the spec for what they
        name, each read before anything it covers is changed. It is injected
        into the system template wherever SPEC_READING is written, and may
        itself use every placeholder but SPEC_READING, which in it is left as
        written. One left with nothing but blank space leaves SPEC_READING
        filled in with nothing. Like the templates, each project has its own,
        saved with its data, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, in
        spec-reading.md beside them, and edited in the
        @{SettingsWindowScope}; with no file yet the project uses its default.

    codeToSpec:
        The code-to-spec prompt is given to a Code task sent to Spec, as the
        @{PromptSendingScope} says, after the Spec instructions. It may use
        every placeholder the instructions may, filled in the same way, and
        two of its own: CODE_PROMPT, filled in with the code task's prompt as
        it was typed, and CODE_RESULT, with the code task's final output, or
        with a line saying the code task left none. What fills them in is
        taken as text, never read as Piton. Like the spec-reading prompt, each
        project has its own, saved with its data in code-to-spec.md beside the
        templates, and edited in the @{SettingsWindowScope}; with no file yet
        the project uses its default.

        The spec-to-code prompt is given in the same way to the code step a
        Chain prompt hands on to, after the Code instructions, with
        SPEC_PROMPT and SPEC_RESULT, the Chain prompt as it was typed and its
        spec step's final output, saved in spec-to-code.md.

    saving:
        Each project has its own system template, instructions, and injected
        prompts, saved with its data, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, a
        Markdown file each, system.md for the system template, code.md,
        combined.md for Chain, spec.md, and ask.md for the modes, and edited
        in the @{SettingsWindowScope}. One with no file yet gives its default.

    understandingFile:
        Each Code, Chain, or Spec task has an understanding file: the short
        list of constraints the harness has taken from the spec for it, which
        the @{RightSidebarScope} shows as it changes. It is saved
        beside the task's history record, with the same name and the
        extension `.understanding.md`, written by the harness itself. Nothing
        else writes it, and nothing is there until the harness writes it. Each
        constraint links to the compiled reference file it comes from, never
        to the spec's source.

    defaults:
        The defaults are the prompts saved in this application's own
        repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, named as a
        project's are. They are the source of truth for the defaults, and are
        baked into the application when it is built, so a build always ships
        with whatever those files say, and changing them changes the defaults
        the next build has. A build can't be made without them.

        The system template's default says what the project is, where its
        code is and where its spec is, each on a paragraph of its own, so the
        one a run can't see goes, that each prompt starts with a
        <task-instructions> block saying what that prompt is for and what it
        may change, and then SPEC_READING on a paragraph of its own. It holds
        no fluency.

        The spec-reading prompt's default says:

        \\
        Read the spec from its compiled reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter.

        Never read the .pi source under ${SPEC_LOCATION} to learn what the spec says; that is only where edits to the spec go.

        Before executing anything, read the spec it touches. Links to ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/... in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one you need before changing anything it covers. Don't re-read something you've already read.
        \\

        The Spec and Chain defaults have, after what the mode is for, on a
        paragraph of its own:

        \\
        Before creating or editing any .pi file, read ${PITON_FLUENCY_FILE} once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.
        \\

        and then, on another:

        \\
        Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, not by reading the source again.
        \\

        The Code, Chain, and Spec defaults then end with, on a paragraph of
        its own:

        \\
        Before changing anything, write the constraints this task must meet to ${UNDERSTANDING_FILE}, and keep it current as you read more of the spec. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.
        \\

        The Ask default says what a question is for, and that it changes
        nothing, and, on a paragraph of its own, that SPEC_LOCATION is the
        spec's Piton source, there for `piton slice`, which the question reads
        the spec through, read only and never edited, and never read directly
        to learn what the spec says. Since a question can see the spec
        location, that paragraph is always sent with it.

        The Ask default then says, on a paragraph of its own, how an answer
        hands back prompts and questions in the forms the
        @{AskConversationScope} shows as cards:

        \\
        When your answer suggests a prompt for the user to send, write it as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, one of `code`, `chain`, `spec`, `ask`, or `freeform`, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text, ready to send. When you need the user to answer something before you can go on, write the question as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`, the question on its first lines and then, if there are answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Use these blocks only for prompts and questions meant for the user, never for code or examples.
        \\

        The Spec and Chain
        defaults never name the code location, and the Code default names the
        spec location only on a paragraph of its own, which goes where the run
        can't see it.

        The defaults are only where a project starts, and what resetting a
        prompt puts back. A project whose prompts were saved before a default
        changed keeps them as they are.

content.text:
I've specced a way for Ask answers to hand back prompts and questions that Suspense shows as cards. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` succeeds inside the container now. The `.piton` and code-location mounts from earlier are live, so I checked the result in the refreshed reference.

**The format:** the agent writes fenced code blocks with a special info string. Markdown already handles fences, so this streams well, and older answers still read sensibly.
- **Prompt:** ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ```` holding the prompt text. The mode can be `code`, `chain`, `spec`, `ask` or `freeform`.
- **Question back to you:** ```` ```suspense-question ```` with the question on its first lines, then optional answers, one per `- ` line.

**Prompt card:**
- It sits in the answer where the block was. It's a raised box tinted the mode's colour, headed with the mode's icon and a name such as "Code prompt", with the text shown as written.
- It has two buttons, **Copy** and **Send to prompt**.
- Send to prompt fills the chat input, selects the mode's tab and focuses the input with the cursor at the end. It never sends; you read, edit and send it yourself.
- Anything you'd already typed is set aside and comes back once that prompt is sent or cleared. Attachments stay. The button reads "Sent to prompt" with a check for 2 seconds.
- A missing or unknown mode gives a plain "Prompt" card in Ask's colour, and Send to prompt selects Chain.

**Question card:**
- It's tinted Ask's colour, with the question rendered as markdown and one button per offered answer.
- Clicking an answer asks it straight away as the next question, in the same conversation. The question is quoted, followed by your pick.
- A card can be answered only once. Your pick is highlighted, the other buttons are disabled, and the pick is saved with the question so it survives reopening the project.
- A card with no answers has no buttons; you just reply as normal.

**In both:** a block that's still streaming shows as a card with its buttons disabled. A block left unclosed when the answer finishes still becomes a card.

Things I decided that you may want to change:
- I limited this to Ask answers; task output doesn't get cards.
- Picking an answer sends it immediately rather than filling the input first.
- Send to prompt sets your existing text aside rather than appending the card's text to it.

`mode-system-prompts/index.pi` fails `piton format --check`. That's probably the long placeholder list lines, which were already there before this change. I didn't reformat the file.

## What changed in the spec, and the anchors the code should follow

- **`AskConversationShape.suggestedPrompts` (new):** detect `suspense-prompt [mode]` fenced blocks in the answer's markdown and render them as prompt cards with Copy and Send to prompt, behaving as described above. Send to prompt goes through `ChatInputScope`: set the text, select the tab, focus the input, set aside existing text as when editing a queued prompt, and keep attachments.
- **`AskConversationShape.askingBack` (new):** detect `suspense-question` blocks and render them as question cards with one button per `- ` line. A click asks the question-quote plus the pick as the next question in the same conversation, the way `PromptSendingScope` sends any question. Save the pick with the question whose answer holds the card. A card can be answered once.
